Onyx
ON-iks
n.
Greek onyx, “fingernail, claw”; named for the stone’s color resembling a fingernail. Hebrew shoham, identified with onyx (a variety of chalcedony with parallel banded colors, often black-and-white, brown-and-white, or red-and-white); used in the high priest’s breastplate and ephod.

Biblical Definition

Onyx (Hebrew shoham) is one of the precious stones identified by Scripture with particular theological-priestly significance, used in the high priest’s vestments to represent the twelve tribes of Israel before the LORD perpetually. Exodus 28:9-12 prescribes the use: and thou shalt take two onyx stones, and grave on them the names of the children of Israel: Six of their names on one stone, and the other six names of the rest on the other stone, according to their birth. With the work of an engraver in stone, like the engravings of a signet, shalt thou engrave the two stones with the names of the children of Israel: thou shalt make them to be set in ouches of gold. And thou shalt put the two stones upon the shoulders of the ephod for stones of memorial unto the children of Israel: and Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD upon his two shoulders for a memorial. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the engraving: the names of the twelve tribes are graven into the stones with the permanence of signet-engraving, an indelible marking. Second, the location: the stones are set on the shoulders of the ephod—the place of bearing burdens, the structural-supporting region of the body. The high priest carries the names of the twelve tribes on his shoulders, perpetually bearing them as he ministers before the LORD. Third, the function: for a memorial—the stones cause the names to be perpetually remembered before the LORD’s face as the high priest stands in His presence. The onyx stones are therefore a covenantal-priestly device by which the people of God are kept perpetually before His face through their representative who bears their names on his shoulders into the holy place. The typological fulfillment in Christ is unmistakable. Christ as our Great High Priest perpetually bears the names of His people on His shoulders into the presence of the Father: seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession (Heb 4:14); wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them (Heb 7:25); for Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us (Heb 9:24). The names of the redeemed are graven into the very being of the great High Priest who bears them perpetually before the Father; the Aaronic onyx stones were the shadow whose substance is Christ Himself bearing His people before God in His unceasing intercession. Onyx also appears at the beginning and the end of Scripture: in the land of Havilah at creation (Gen 2:12, and the gold of that land is good: there is bdellium and the onyx stone), and among the foundation stones of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20). The stone traverses the canonical arc from creation to consummation, from Eden’s good land to the city of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ONYX as a semi-pellucid gem with various colors of veins, especially black and white in parallel layers; in scripture, the stone used for the two engraved stones on the shoulders of the high priest’s ephod, bearing the names of the twelve tribes for a perpetual memorial before the LORD.

expand to see more

ONYX, n. — A semi-pellucid gem, with variously colored veins, often black and white in parallel layers; a variety of chalcedony. In scripture, used in the high priest’s ephod (Ex 28:9-12) and among the foundation stones of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20).

EPHOD, n. — A piece of dress worn by the Jewish priests; the outer garment of the high priest, on the shoulders of which the onyx stones were set.

Key Scripture

Exodus 28:9-12 — "And thou shalt take two onyx stones, and grave on them the names of the children of Israel: Six of their names on one stone, and the other six names of the rest on the other stone... And thou shalt put the two stones upon the shoulders of the ephod for stones of memorial unto the children of Israel: and Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD upon his two shoulders for a memorial."

Genesis 2:12 — "And the gold of that land is good: there is bdellium and the onyx stone."

Hebrews 7:25 — "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."

Revelation 21:19-20 — "And the foundations of the wall of the city were garnished with all manner of precious stones... the fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius..."

Modern Corruption

The onyx-doctrine is corrupted in much contemporary preaching by the general loss of typological reading that no longer traces the high priest’s ephod-stones to their Christological fulfillment in the great High Priest who perpetually bears His people’s names before the Father—and by the inverse over-allegorization that extracts arbitrary spiritual meaning from each gemstone without the typological-Christological grounding the NT itself provides.

expand to see more

The general loss of typological reading affects the onyx-doctrine as it does the broader tabernacle-and-priesthood typology. The two engraved onyx stones on the high priest’s shoulders are taught (where they are taught at all) as ancient priestly detail without serious tracing to their fulfillment in Christ the Great High Priest who perpetually bears His people’s names before the Father. The recovery is the recovery of the typology, with Hebrews 7–10’s sustained Christ-as-high-priest argument providing the controlling framework. Christ is the substance of which the Aaronic priesthood was the shadow; the onyx stones bearing the names of the twelve tribes typify the substantive reality that Christ Himself carries the names of His redeemed people perpetually into the presence of God in His unceasing intercession. The pastoral application is direct and tender: the saint’s name is borne on the shoulders of his great High Priest perpetually before the Father; he is never forgotten, never absent from the holy place, never out of the High Priest’s remembrance. The recovery of the doctrine is the recovery of one of the deepest pastoral consolations Scripture supplies.

The opposite corruption is the over-allegorization that extracts arbitrary spiritual meaning from each gemstone (the onyx specifically signifying something the text does not specify, with imagined correspondences between particular stones and particular tribes, particular virtues, particular events of salvation history) without the typological-Christological grounding the NT itself authorizes. Tabernacle-allegorizing of this kind, when it loses its biblical anchor, becomes preacher-invention rather than disciplined typological reading. The biblical pattern is precise. Typological reading is appropriate where the NT itself does it (Christ as Great High Priest is the controlling framework for tabernacle typology); typological inference is appropriate where it is grounded in the NT’s own pattern; bare allegorization of details the NT does not address is to be avoided. The onyx-typology, well-anchored in the Hebrews high-priest doctrine, stands; the imagined gemstone-correspondences of impressive-but-ungrounded preaching do not. The recovery is disciplined typological reading: rich enough to draw out the pastoral substance, restrained enough not to invent meaning the Spirit did not put there.

Hebrew Roots

Greek onyx (fingernail, claw—named for the stone’s color); Hebrew shoham; the precious stone used for the two engraved stones on the shoulders of the high priest’s ephod, bearing the names of the twelve tribes for a perpetual memorial before the LORD; typologically fulfilled in Christ the Great High Priest who bears His people’s names perpetually before the Father.

expand to see more

Hebrew shoham (H7718) — onyx (Gen 2:12; Ex 25:7; 28:9-12, 20; 35:9, 27; 39:6, 13; 1 Chr 29:2; Job 28:16; Ezek 28:13).

Greek onyx — fingernail, claw (the etymological source of English onyx, from the stone’s color).

Greek sardonyx (G4557) — sardonyx (Rev 21:20; the fifth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem).

Hebrew ephod (H646) — ephod (the high priest’s vestment on whose shoulders the onyx stones were set).

Usage

"The two onyx stones on the high priest’s shoulders bore the names of the twelve tribes for a perpetual memorial before the LORD."

"Christ as our Great High Priest perpetually bears the names of His people on His shoulders into the presence of the Father—Heb 7:25, ever living to make intercession."

"The saint’s pastoral consolation: his name is borne on the shoulders of his great High Priest perpetually before the Father; he is never forgotten, never absent from the holy place."
